E.6 Full Benchmarking Results
We report the full benchmarking results and experimental details on A100.
Baselines We compare against reference implementations for exact attention from PyTorch/HuggingFace
and Megatron, approximate attention, and sparse attention. For approximate attention, we compare against
reference implementations of Reformer [51], Local Attention [68], Linformer Attention [84], Smyrf [19], and
LongShortFormer (LSFormer) [94]. For sparse attention, we compare against reference implementations of
Block-Sparse Attention form OpenAI [11], Longformer[3], and BigBird Attention [92]. For the approximate
and sparse attention, we use a compression ratio of 1/8, or a compressed sequence length of 256, whichever is
smaller.
Setup We measure runtime and memory usage of the attention computation with 8 heads of dimension 64,
and batch size 16 on a machine with one A100 GPU with 40 GB of GPU HBM. We vary sequence length
in our experiments. We compute attention on random vectors forQ, K, and V (we do not measure the
projection from the hidden layer). For dropout, we use dropout 0.1; for masking, we use a padding mask
with uniformly-random mask lengths between the total sequence length and the total sequence length minus
20. To measure runtime, we take the average of 100 measurements of the attention call. We only measure
memory footprint once, since it does not vary between runs.

evidence.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
evidence.text:
Runtime. Figure 3 (left) reports the runtime in milliseconds of the forward + backward pass ofFlashAt-
tention and block-sparse FlashAttentioncompared to the baselines in exact, approximate, and sparse
attention (exact numbers in Appendix E). Runtime grows quadratically with sequence length, butFlashAt-
tention runs signiﬁcantly faster thanexact attention baselines, up to 3 faster than the PyTorch
implementation. The runtimes of many approximate/sparse attention mechanisms grow linearly with se-
quence length, but FlashAttention still runs faster than approximate and sparse attention for short
sequences due to fewer memory accesses. Theapproximate attentionruntimes begin to cross over with
FlashAttention at sequences between 512 and 1024. On the other hand, block-sparseFlashAttention
is faster than all implementations of exact, sparse, and approximate attention that we know of, across all
sequence lengths.
Memory Footprint. Figure 3 (right) shows the memory footprint ofFlashAttention and block-sparse
FlashAttentioncompared to various exact, approximate, and sparse attention baselines.FlashAttention
and block-sparse FlashAttentionhave the same memory footprint, which grows linearly with sequence
length. FlashAttention is up to 20 more memory eﬃcient thanexact attentionbaselines, and is more
memory-eﬃcient than theapproximate attentionbaselines. All other algorithms except for Linformer run
out of memory on an A100 GPU before 64K, andFlashAttention is still 2 more eﬃcient than Linformer.
5 Limitations and Future Directions
We discuss limitations of our approach and future directions. Related work is given in Appendix A.
Compiling to CUDA.Our current approach to building IO-aware implementations of attention requires
writing a new CUDA kernel for each new attention implementation. This requires writing the attention
algorithm in a considerably lower-level language than PyTorch, and requires signiﬁcant engineering eﬀort.
Implementations may also not be transferrable across GPU architectures. These limitations suggest the
need for a method that supports writing attention algorithms in a high-level language (e.g., PyTorch), and
compiling to IO-aware implementations in CUDA—similar to eﬀorts such as Halide in image processing [70].
IO-Aware Deep Learning. We believe that the IO-aware approach can extend beyond attention.
Attention is the most memory-intensive computation in Transformers, but every layer in a deep network
touches GPU HBM. We hope our work inspires IO-aware implementations of additional modules. We discuss
these potential extensions in Appendix D.
Multi-GPU IO-Aware Methods.Our IO-aware implementation of attention is optimal within con-
stants for computing attention on a single GPU. However, the attention computation may be parallelizable

evidence.text:
### D — Fused attention (SDPA)

The baseline materializes the full Tq × Tk score matrix before softmax; at T=2048, batch 8, 4 heads this matrix alone is `8 × 4 × 2048 × 2048`. `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` (SDPA) fuses the computation so the full matrix is never written out.

Measured on a full forward pass (batch 8, bf16, 4 layers / 4 heads / 256 dims):

| n_kv_head | impl | T=128 | T=512 | T=2048 | peak mem (T=2048) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | baseline (full matrix) | 3.73 ms | 4.63 ms | 53.91 ms | 604.3 MB |
| 4 | **fused (SDPA)** | 3.40 ms | 3.19 ms | 19.28 ms | 144.3 MB |
| 4 | chunked (online softmax) | 6.26 ms | 14.31 ms | 131.66 ms | 185.3 MB |
| 1 | baseline (full matrix) | 3.33 ms | 4.45 ms | 51.09 ms | 607.6 MB |
| 1 | **fused (SDPA)** | 3.09 ms | 3.03 ms | **13.88 ms** | **143.6 MB** |
| 1 | chunked (online softmax) | 6.12 ms | 13.65 ms | 129.37 ms | 188.6 MB |

At T=2048 the fused path is 3.68× faster (n_kv_head=1) with peak memory 607.6 → 143.6 MB. The gap grows with sequence length; at T=128 both paths are in the fixed-overhead regime and show no difference.

Three points worth noting:

- This is PyTorch's fused entry point, not the FlashAttention kernel itself. On this machine the backend that actually runs is cuDNN (`FLASH_ATTENTION` is not built, `is_flash_attention_available()` returns `False`), and the speedup holds only in bf16 — in fp32 the fused backends are mostly unavailable for grouped-query shapes.
- The default dispatcher silently selects `MATH` for grouped-query shapes (21.73 ms / 1257.3 MB); pinning the fused backend explicitly gives 1.292 ms / 41.25 MB (16.8×). The code therefore pins the backend list rather than relying on the dispatcher.

Figure 5: Attention forward speed on A100 GPU
Just running the same implementation on H100 GPUs (using no special instructions to make use of new
features such as TMA and 4th-gen Tensor Cores), we obtain up to 335 TFLOPs/s (Fig. 7). We expect that by
using new instructions, we can obtain another 1.5x-2x speedup on H100 GPUs. We leave that to future work.
4.2 End-to-end Performance
We measure the training throughput of GPT-style models with either 1.3B or 2.7B parameters, on 8×A100
80GB SXM. As shown in Table 1,FlashAttention-2 yields 2.8× speedup compared to a baseline without
FlashAttention and 1.3× speedup compared toFlashAttention-2, reaching up to 225 TFLOPs/s per A100
GPU.
Note that we calculate the FLOPs by the formula, following Megatron-LM [16] (and many other papers
and libraries):
6·seqlen·number of params+ 12·number of layers·hidden dim·seqlen2.
The first term accounts for the FLOPs due to weight–input multiplication, and the second term accounts for
the FLOPs due to attention. However, one can argue that the second term should be halved, as with causal
mask we only need to compute approximately half the number of elements in attention. We choose to follow
the formula from the literature (without dividing the attention FLOPs by 2) for consistency.

evidence.title: mygpt / README.md
evidence.text:
# mygpt

A character-level GPT (3.2M parameters) used as a controlled testbed for measuring the effect of five common training/inference optimizations. Each optimization is implemented as an independent switch: the baseline and the modified run differ by exactly one flag, so any difference between them can be attributed to that single change. Every number in this document is backed by raw measurements committed under `results/*.json`.

## Results at a glance

| # | Optimization | Measured effect |
|---|---|---|
| A | LayerNorm → RMSNorm | Parameters −2,304; peak training memory 365.7 → 329.6 MB (−10%); step time unchanged |
| B | KV cache | Generation 30.5× faster at batch 32; 0.98× (no gain) at batch 1 |
| C | GQA / MQA | Per-sequence KV cache 12.0 → 6.0 → 3.0 → 1.5 MB (−87.5% for MQA) |
| D | Fused attention (SDPA) | 3.68× faster at T=2048; peak memory 607.6 → 143.6 MB |
| E | Paged KV cache | Reserved-memory waste 93.8% → 16.45%; shared prefix 2.0 → 0.25 MB |

## Purpose

The primary goal is to quantify, through controlled before/after experiments, how much each of five widely used optimizations actually improves a Transformer model, and at what cost. The emphasis is on the measurements and their interpretation rather than on building a language model or a training stack.

A secondary goal is understanding the Transformer architecture itself: causal self-attention, multi-head attention, the MLP, residual connections, normalization, and positional embeddings.

## Model and setup

```
input "F" "i" "r" "s" "t"  →  token ids (B, T)
  │
  ├─ wte  token embedding     (65 × 256)
  └─ wpe  position embedding  (128 × 256)   →  summed to (B, T, 256)
  │
  ▼   repeated 4× (each Block)
  ├─ normalization              ← A switch: LayerNorm / RMSNorm
  ├─ causal self-attention      ← B (KV cache) / C (GQA) / D (attention path)
  ├─ residual add
  ├─ normalization
  ├─ MLP  256 → 1024 → 256
  └─ residual add
  │
  ▼
  final normalization → Linear(256 → 65)  →  scores over 65 characters
                                             (weights shared with wte)
```

evidence.text:
`out/` (model weights, ~13 MB each) is excluded by `.gitignore`; `results/` (JSON, a few KB) is committed.

## Limitations

- This is not a usable language model: 3.2M parameters, character-level, 1.1 MB of text, 3,000 steps. It is a measurement vehicle.
- Single run, single seed, single laptop GPU. Validation-loss differences around 0.005 are noise.
- The 30.5× is not a universal constant; it is the intersection of O(T²) vs O(T) generation on this hardware at batch 32.
- The architecture is GPT-2 style (no RoPE, no SwiGLU, no gradient checkpointing). The five optimizations are introduced in isolation.
- Attention runs through PyTorch's fused entry point, not the FlashAttention kernel; the speedup is bf16-only.
- The paged KV cache is a Python-level proof of concept (no copy-on-write, no scheduler, attention still gathers blocks back into a contiguous tensor).
- The default KV cache remains the plainest `torch.cat` version; the paged path coexists in `paged_kv.py`.
- Repeated measurements vary by 1.6%–7.7%, and timing is taken on a thermally-throttling laptop.

**Code and data**

- [karpathy/nanoGPT](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT) — architecture, weight initialization, and residual scaling follow its approach. This repository differs in five ways: attention split into three projections (required for GQA), switchable normalization, KV-cache generation (absent in upstream nanoGPT), three switchable attention paths, and an additional paged KV-cache implementation.
- [karpathy/char-rnn](https://github.com/karpathy/char-rnn) — the TinyShakespeare dataset (≈1.1 MB).

# Prefill 与 Decode

> 状态：AI整理草稿，未获人工逐项确认。本文是完整知识词条，不是论文逐字原文。

## 定义与用途

# FlashAttention 与 IO 优化

> 状态：AI整理草稿，未获人工逐项确认。本文是完整知识词条，不是论文逐字原文。

## 定义与用途

FlashAttention针对精确注意力的数据搬运开销进行优化，利用分块和片上存储减少HBM读写及中间矩阵物化。

## 工作机制

普通实现可能将T×T分数和概率写入显存。FlashAttention按Q/K/V块计算，结合在线softmax更新中间统计与输出，避免保存完整概率矩阵。原算法是精确注意力的IO优化，不是通过稀疏化或近似softmax省略任意关系。

## 适用条件与易混淆点

浮点累加顺序不同可产生容差内数值差异，精确算法不等于逐bit相同。二次注意力算术未因省去矩阵物化而自动变成线性；收益依序列长度、硬件与内核限制而变。

## 关联知识

PyTorch SDPA 与后端选择、分块注意力与在线 Softmax、性能测量、正确性与适用条件

FlashAttention针对精确注意力的数据搬运开销进行优化，利用分块和片上存储减少HBM读写及中间矩阵物化。

## 工作机制

普通实现可能将T×T分数和概率写入显存。FlashAttention按Q/K/V块计算，结合在线softmax更新中间统计与输出，避免保存完整概率矩阵。原算法是精确注意力的IO优化，不是通过稀疏化或近似softmax省略任意关系。

## 适用条件与易混淆点

浮点累加顺序不同可产生容差内数值差异，精确算法不等于逐bit相同。二次注意力算术未因省去矩阵物化而自动变成线性；收益依序列长度、硬件与内核限制而变。

# 分块注意力与在线 Softmax

> 状态：AI整理草稿，未获人工逐项确认。本文是完整知识词条，不是论文逐字原文。

## 定义与用途

在线softmax用运行中的最大值和归一化量合并分块结果，使注意力不必保存完整分数矩阵。它不是逐块独立softmax后直接平均。

## 工作机制

已处理分块保留最大值m、指数和l、未归一化加权和o。新块最大值m_b、指数和l_b、加权和o_b到来时，m'=max(m,m_b)，l'=exp(m−m')l+exp(m_b−m')l_b，o'=exp(m−m')o+exp(m_b−m')o_b，最终输出o'/l'。旧块必须按新最大值重缩放。

## 适用条件与易混淆点

掩码和空块需专门处理，不能对全−∞行机械使用上述式子。Python教学分块代码不等同于融合GPU内核；减少峰值中间存储也不保证端到端更快。

## 关联知识

FlashAttention 与 IO 优化、PyTorch SDPA 与后端选择
